summary:
TerraTwin: Explainable Terrain Analog Discovery for the Moon and Mars

We developed TerraTwin, an interactive platform that identifies and explains terrain analogs between selected locations on the Moon or Mars and the Atacama Desert in Chile. It analyzes terrain features—including mean slope, robust elevation relief, and slope variability—using standardized measurements from 5 km grid cells. Users can configure target regions, select terrain features, explore ranked Earth candidates, and inspect side-by-side comparisons through interactive maps and visual summaries.

TerraTwin addresses the challenge by providing a data-driven way to identify Earth locations with terrain characteristics similar to potential exploration areas on the Moon and Mars. Rather than simply presenting a similarity score, it explains how each candidate compares across the selected features, helping users understand both similarities and differences.

This is important because Earth-based terrain analogs can support the planning and interpretation of planetary exploration activities. By making terrain comparisons accessible and explainable, TerraTwin can help researchers and mission planners explore potential locations for field studies and test scenarios. It also highlights where Earth's available reference terrain may not provide a close match, helping communicate the limits of analog-based comparisons.
details:
Project Details — TerraTwin

TerraTwin is an interactive terrain analog discovery platform that helps users identify and understand Earth locations with terrain characteristics similar to selected regions on the Moon and Mars. The current study compares the Moon's South Pole and Mars's Jezero Crater against the Atacama Desert in Chile, our initial Earth reference region.

What does it do and how does it work?

TerraTwin processes digital elevation models from three planetary data sources: NASA's SRTM data for Earth, Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) data for the Moon, and Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) data for Mars. The terrain datasets are resampled to a common 500-meter resolution and summarized into 5 km grid cells.

For each eligible cell, TerraTwin calculates three terrain features: mean slope, robust elevation relief (P90–P10), and slope variability. It filters out cells with insufficient data coverage, then standardizes feature differences using the Earth reference region's median and robust spread. A Euclidean distance is calculated to rank the closest available Atacama candidates for each planetary target cell.

Users can select a planetary target, choose terrain features, configure the number of candidates, and explore ranked results through interactive maps, summaries, and feature-by-feature comparisons.

Benefits and intended impact

TerraTwin makes planetary terrain comparisons more accessible, transparent, and explainable. It can help researchers, educators, and mission-planning teams explore potential Earth field-study locations for terrain-focused investigations and test scenarios. Instead of presenting only a similarity score, it shows which terrain properties contribute to a match and where important differences remain.

Tools and technologies

The project uses Python, Rasterio, GDAL, NumPy, and geospatial processing tools for terrain preparation and feature extraction. DuckDB and SQL power the analytical queries, candidate ranking, and discovery workflow. The web application provides an interactive interface with maps and visual summaries, and is deployed on Vercel. NASA's Global Imagery Browse Services (GIBS) supports planetary map visualization.

Creativity and design considerations

TerraTwin combines planetary geospatial datasets, a configurable ranking engine, and explainable results in one interactive workflow. Its creative contribution is making the comparison process inspectable: users can change the features being compared and see how the candidate rankings respond.

We considered differences in source resolution, spatial coverage, missing-data quality, terrain measurement scales, and the limitations of comparing different planetary bodies. Absolute elevation values are not directly compared because planetary vertical reference systems differ. We also distinguish terrain similarity from overall environmental or mission suitability.

The current Earth reference library contains only the Atacama Desert. The resulting distances are standardized feature differences, not probabilities or percentages of similarity. Gravity, regolith composition, radiation, and temperature are not included in the ranking. TerraTwin is therefore an exploratory terrain-comparison tool, not a landing-site safety assessment.
